title: PhoneValue-Bench: A Multimodal Benchmark and Datasets for Consumer Smartphone Recommerce Valuation
authors: Zihan Deng, Jun Gao
abstract: As consumer smartphone recommerce scales, buyers must quote binding repurchase prices from seller-uploaded multi-view photos and diagnostic screenshots before devices reach the warehouse. Accurate remote valuation requires fusing noisy cosmetic evidence with identity, battery, lock, and channel risk from screenshots and staff forms, since an error in any modality changes both grade and payout. title: ElectroChemLLM: A Multimodal LLM Pipeline for High-Fidelity Electrochemical Informatics
authors: Dikshya Mohanty, Manoj Praveen Nandigama, Kuldeepsinh Raj et al.
abstract: Electrochemistry is central to solving many modern-day challenges, including energy storage systems for a sustainable future, and its advancement relies heavily on the data from past findings. Existing automated pipelines are limited by text-only architectures, context fragmentation, and numerical hallucinations - collectively preventing accurate, large-scale curation of property databases. title: Words Before Pixels: Selective Modality Routing for Vision-Language Model Unlearning
authors: Laura Yao, Haochen Zhang, Jinhao Duan et al.
abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) unlearning is often treated as an objective-design problem: given multimodal forget data, the goal is to optimize a loss that removes undesirable behavior while preserving retained capabilities. We argue that this view overlooks an equally important data-centric question: how should each forget example be represented before optimization? title: LoRAForge: Co-Designing Post-Hoc Compression and Execution for Efficient Multi-LoRA Serving
authors: Shenghui Li, Thiemo Voigt
abstract: Multi-LoRA serving allows many task-specific adapters to share a common base model, but scaling to large adapter fleets introduces substantial storage, loading, and execution overheads. Post-hoc compression can reduce the memory footprint of trained LoRA adapters, yet smaller ranks do not automatically translate into faster serving. title: ArSciKids: Arabic Curriculum-Aligned Datasets for Scientific Experiment and Multiple-Choice Question Generation in Primary Education
authors: Taghrid Housari, Massa Rankoussi, Jafar Abdul Majeed et al.
abstract: Despite growing interest in Arabic natural language processing, curriculum-aligned educational resources remain scarce compared with English, and few public datasets for Arabic curriculum content with structured, generation-ready annotations are available, particularly for primary-school science. title: Labadain-MedQA: A Tetun Medical QA Dataset for Fine-Tuning and Evaluating Large Language Models
authors: Gabriel de Jesus, Sérgio Nunes
abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) have created opportunities for cross-lingual transfer of medical knowledge from high-resource to low-resource languages to support access to healthcare information. However, medical question-answering (QA) datasets for fine-tuning and evaluating LLMs remain scarce for Tetun. title: Reading Between the Chapters: A Graph-Free RAG Rebuilt With AI and Human Feedback
authors: Dipto Sumit, Syeda Fabiayee Jahan, Farig Sadeque
abstract: Many questions about a book can only be answered by connecting passages chapters apart, such as a cough heard three times across a horse's life. We introduce CrossChapterQA, 1,853 such questions over 14 public-domain books. Each question lists the two to six chapters it needs (spanning half the book at the median) and the relation linking them, cites evidence from each, and has two independent reference answers graded blind. title: Dual-Axis Policy Entailment: A Benchmark for Policy-Change Reasoning
authors: Charles Chang, Yuen Yuen Ang, Bolun Sun
abstract: Whether a policy shifts domains and, by extension, continues, broadens, narrows, or reverses previous policy is of paramount importance to the study of public policy. title: J-Anchor: Defending Against Prefill Attacks via J-Space Selective Refusal Restoration
authors: Running Yang, Beidi Zhao, Xiaoxiao Li
abstract: Prefill jailbreaks can cause safety-aligned language models to continue an unsafe assistant prefix even when they would refuse the same request under normal decoding. We study how the model's internal harmfulness and refusal signals evolve along this attacker-controlled trajectory. Using the Jacobian lens, we track vocabulary-grounded harmfulness and refusal signals from the assistant header through prefilling and subsequent generation. title: HiGenTrans: Hierarchical LLM Knowledge Transfer for Generative Recommendation
authors: Zhuohang Jiang, Yuxin Chen, Haohao Qu et al.
abstract: Generative recommendation promises to simplify conventional multi-stage recommender systems by generating item Semantic IDs (SIDs) autoregressively. However, two obstacles limit its effective- ness in industrial settings: interaction-only supervision underuses the semantic knowledge encoded in pretrained language models, while beam-search likelihood ranks token sequences rather than directly estimating item relevance. title: AdKnob: Ad Intensity Control and Labeling for LLM-Native Advertising
authors: Woo Jae Kim, Seongho Keum, Joonsung Jeon et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-native advertising has emerged as a viable monetization channel as LLM service providers seek sustainable revenue streams. However, integrating native ads into LLM responses introduces two largely understudied challenges: (1) controlling ad intensity -- how prominently advertising content appears -- and (2) ad labeling -- identifying which segments of the generated text constitute advertising. title: Distinguishing among reasoning levels of GPT 5.5 Pro via a grammar lens benchmark
authors: Emma Graham, Richard Granger
abstract: Does the level of test-time processing effort affect a language model's computational capability? A formal grammar-lens benchmark method, derived from the theory of computation, generates novel data at specified levels, each successively more computationally powerful than the levels below. title: Step-dLLM: Adaptive Step-aware Sparse Attention for Efficient Diffusion LLM Inference
authors: Zhichen Zeng, Xichong Zhang, Junpan Wu et al.
abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate tokens in parallel via iterative denoising, but their bidirectional attention prevents the KV caching used by autoregressive models and recomputes the full attention map at every step, incurring quadratic per-step cost. Existing sparse attention methods for dLLMs construct a sparse mask after an initial full-attention warm-up and reuse it for the remaining steps, while allocating the sparsity budget uniformly across heads. title: Character-Name Concentration in LLM Fiction: Measuring Displacement and Mitigating Repetition
authors: Alejandro Mozo Quesada, Sergio Gálvez Rojas, Francisco López Valverde
abstract: Character names in large language model (LLM) fiction concentrate on a handful of recurrent names such as 'Elara' and 'Elias', a measurable face of AI slop. Existing fixes either require logit access or retraining, or operate per request and cannot control concentration across a corpus. How much prompt-level strategies reduce concentration, and at what cost to name naturalness, has not been systematically measured. title: OntoDoc: Automatically Generating Ontology Resource Descriptions
authors: Juan Guajardo Gutierrez, Mike Tran, Nasim Shirvani Mahdavi et al.
abstract: Knowledge graphs and ontologies form the backbone of structured, machine-readable knowledge representation, yet ontology terms often lack natural language descriptions, limiting their accessibility and reuse. Existing ontology verbalization approaches tend to rely on rule-based or template-driven techniques that operate on strict, formal schema axioms, resulting in rigid verbalizations that fail to convey richer contextual semantics. We present OntoDoc, a multi-agent framework for automatically

title: The Brittle Compass: Navigating LLM Prompt Sensitivity in Slovak Migration Media Discourse
authors: Samuel Harvan, Jaroslav Kopčan, Marek Šuppa et al.
abstract: In this work, we present a case study that explores various tasks centered around the topic of migration in Slovak, a low-resource language, such as topic relevance and geographical relevance classification, and migration source/destination location term extraction. Our results demonstrate that native (Slovak) prompts yield a modest, task-dependent gains, while large models show significant robustness to prompt variations compared to their smaller counterparts. title: Vision-Language Models Are Joint Denoisers in Robotic Action Generation
authors: Xicheng Gong, Wenxuan Song, Chengze Liu et al.
abstract: Diffusion-based vision-language-action (VLA) models cascade pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) with diffusion action experts, but typically restrict the VLM to providing static conditioning. This separation limits how much pretrained perception and reasoning can guide action generation, especially in out-of-distribution settings. title: Capacity Planning for Resource-Constrained Clinical LLM Serving
authors: Yi Tang, Geoffrey Martin, Yiye Zhang et al.
abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) under a fixed accelerator budget requires jointly deciding how computational capacity is allocated across model sizes and how incoming requests are routed across that capacity. Although prior work has extensively studied LLM routing and serving efficiency, the relative importance of fleet composition and routing under resource constraints remains less understood. title: Do Earnings Calls Help Predict Financial Restatements? Evaluating Text Beyond Public Firm Information
authors: Ahmet Efe, Shivank Sapra, Bilal Ahmed
abstract: Financial restatements correct errors in previously published financial reports. Could managers' language in earnings calls warn of them in advance? Comparing 109 calls that precede restatements with 218 matched control calls, we find that the text predicts restatements but adds no detectable ranking gain beyond public firm information. title: Multi-Turn Semantic Caching for Low-Cost LLM Serving
authors: Baran Atalar, Selly Beyene, Xutong Liu et al.
abstract: Semantic caching lowers the cost of serving large language models (LLMs) by reusing stored responses for similar requests. In multi-turn conversations, whether a cached response is acceptable depends on both conversations' histories, which embedding similarity of requests and histories predicts poorly (AUC 0.62--0.74 on five workloads). title: SNAPPerf: Software-Aware Tabular Foundation Model for Retraining-Free Performance Prediction of Configurable Systems
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini, Vadim Okun
abstract: Modern software systems expose hundreds of configuration options whose combinations can substantially affect execution time, memory and energy usage. Measuring software performance resulting from a configuration set requires running a realistic workload. Since the configuration space grows exponentially, exhaustive benchmarking is infeasible. title: Random Is Almost Enough? Stable and Low-Cost Benchmark Compression via BestRand
authors: George Ling, Shanshan Zhong, Lijin Yang et al.
abstract: Benchmark compression reduces the often prohibitive time and cost of model evaluation by evaluating models on a small benchmark subset that closely matches full-benchmark results. To quantify estimation error, we derive an accurate analytical approximation to the error distribution when estimating full-benchmark scores from a subset, showing that most subsets yield small errors, while a few produce much larger errors, resulting in a long-tailed distribution. title: Agent4FreeFem: A Verification-Guided Framework for Autonomous Topology Optimization
authors: Zhipu Cui, Helin Gong, Shengfeng Zhu
abstract: Topology optimization has become an indispensable design tool in the aerospace, automotive, and mechanical engineering industries. Yet bringing a new problem from its description to an optimized result remains slow, expert-dependent, and unreliable: the workflow spans many manually connected stages, each new problem requires solver code to be written and debugged manually, and such code often fails or yields incorrect results. We present Agent4FreeFem, a pipeline driven by a large language model

title: Learning What to Ask and What to Believe: Distilling a Variational Bayesian Agent into Language Models
authors: Baichuan Li, Yanling Chang, Alfredo Garcia
abstract: Interactive tasks such as eliciting a user's preferences or diagnosing a hidden mechanism require an agent to track its uncertainty over a latent state, ask informative questions and act on the answers. title: Self-Refining Prompt Induction for Streaming Text-to-SQL
authors: Gaetano Rossiello, Alfio Gliozzo, Nandana Mihindukulasooriya et al.
abstract: Text-to-SQL assistants for streaming engines must handle dialect-specific types, windowing rules, and temporal semantics, including constructs poorly handled by generic prompts. We present Self-Refining Prompt Induction (SRPI), an offline method that converts generation failures into reusable dialect instructions while keeping model weights fixed. title: Designing Behavioral Profiles for Language Model Simulation of Out-of-Distribution Human Behavior
authors: Robin Na, Kehang Zhu, Logan Cross et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, but which descriptions of people improve prediction when experimental designs change remains unclear. We develop a framework that draws candidate behavioral features from the literature and constructs profiles from earlier human experiments. title: Agentic Context Management for Multi-Turn Human-AI Conversations
authors: Matthew Ho, Chenglong Wang, Baolin Peng et al.
abstract: LLMs degrade in multi-turn conversation partly because of context pollution: the model's own earlier outputs stay in context and anchor later turns, so an early misreading of the user's intent can persist after the user corrects it. Assistant omission (AO), dropping every assistant message, removes this pollution but fails when interaction is referential: later turns refer back to drafts, decisions, and tool-call results that exist only in assistant turns. title: Unsatz: Evaluating Scientific Discovery Without a Given Ansatz
authors: Ethan Ji, Wei Wang, Yizhou Sun
abstract: Before a scientist fits any parameter, they must decide what the model contains: which quantities exist, which are hidden, how they interact, and how they are measured. Physicists call such a trial form an ansatz. Benchmarks for automated equation discovery mostly supply it, by fixing the variables, a library of candidate terms, or a law to be modified. title: Zero-Gated Cross-Attention
authors: Basavaraj R M, Manav Verma
abstract: Injecting non-text modalities into frozen language models often introduces early optimization instability, making it difficult to separate architectural gains from transient training dynamics. We introduce Inductively Gated Cross-Attention (IGCA), a zero-initialized cross-attention bridge that preserves pretrained model behavior at initialization while enabling gradual multimodal conditioning. title: RECITE: Revising Eligibility Criteria Incorporating Textual Evidence
authors: Russell Ro, Reza Abbasi-Asl
abstract: Overly restrictive eligibility criteria contribute to widespread enrollment failure in clinical trials, yet published recommendations for how specific criteria should be broadened remain disconnected from trial design at scale. We introduce RECITE (Revising Eligibility Criteria Incorporating Textual Evidence), a framework for automated discovery, extraction, and implementation of evidence-based eligibility criteria revisions. title: Context as Infrastructure: Knowledge Compilation for Retrieval in Agentic Systems with Harnesses
authors: Zhichang Yu, Baining Cao, Sbaaoui Idriss et al.
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation is becoming agentic. A search harness writes queries, reads results, reformulates, and decides when to stop. This largely solves accuracy: a harness with only BM25/grep and MiniMax M3 answers 85% of BrowseComp-Plus and 91% on multi-hop FRAMES in our runs, without compiled or vector indexes. title: Flide: Accelerating Decision Inference with Exact State Forking
authors: Bobo Li, Jiajia Song, Hao Fei et al.
abstract: Decision models such as Jev have emerged as a highly promising paradigm for LLM agent systems, providing lightweight and reliable categorical reasoning for rapid System One execution. However, existing generation-oriented inference engines fail to support these workloads effectively, suffering from severe prefix recomputation overheads or distorted output probabilities. title: TradeWar: A Benchmark for Execution-Grounded Trade Negotiation with Adaptive LLM Agents
authors: Xiangyu Kong, Ruirui Yang, Xia Hou
abstract: Multi-turn negotiation remains a challenging problem for large language model (LLM) agents. While LLMs can conduct natural-language dialogue, existing benchmarks predominantly assess only agreement rates, overlooking whether negotiated commitments actually create value once executed. authors: Shuyang Zhang
abstract: An agent that must call several tools to fulfill a request fails when the tool retriever omits any one of them, yet tool retrievers are mostly built and evaluated on queries requiring a single tool. We compare representatives of six retrieval structures (flat lexical and dense retrieval, LLM query decomposition, LLM-navigated hierarchies, server-then-tool matching, dependency graphs, and trained set-level retrievers) across two multi-tool testbeds: 345 AppWorld queries with expert dependency lab

title: Real Computation or Merely Naming? A Pre-Registered Mechanism Audit of 25 Cognitive-Architecture Modules in an LLM-Based Agent System
authors: Peter Chen, Ni Zhang, Ying Xu et al.
abstract: Agent systems built on local large language models are increasingly marketed through the vocabulary of cognitive architecture: modules named global workspace, theory of mind, causal reasoning, or active inference are listed as features, and the presence of the name is taken as the presence of the mechanism. title: ORION: An Outcome-Driven LLM Advisor for RL-Based Multi-Domain 6G Slice Placement
authors: Mahmoud S. Mayaleh, Fetia Bannour, Nour-El-Houda Yellas
abstract: Deploying 6G network slices across administrative domains requires an online decision for each arriving request: which domain hosts each virtual network function, how traffic crosses domain boundaries, and whether the slice is admitted. This joint decision problem is NP-hard under continuous arrivals. authors: Jinkyeong Choi, Chaebin Jeong, Junsung Jeon et al.
abstract: Recursive textual memory can carry earlier errors into later updates, yet task performance alone does not establish memory reliability. We define self-consistency bias as the persistence of incorrect claims already present in the incoming memory. title: When Safety Checks Become Privacy Risks: A Privacy-Preserving Paradigm for LLM Agent Safety Auditing
authors: Yixiang Luo, Ziheng Ma, Ke Chang et al.
abstract: Large language model agents interact with online services through tool calls that may access private data or perform sensitive actions. Specialized providers can supply and maintain pre-execution safety auditing capabilities for agent operators. However, sending task descriptions, call arguments, and interaction histories to an external auditor may expose sensitive user information. title: Ask on Demand: Targeted Peer Communication for Parallel Agentic Systems
authors: Haofu Yang, Hongyang Yin, Ran Bi et al.
abstract: Parallel LLM agents tackle complex tasks by exploring multiple trajectories, yet useful discoveries remain isolated in individual execution histories. Existing sharing methods often select or summarize information before other agents' needs become clear, potentially overlooking details that become important later. title: Operon-S1: a fast decision controller for long-horizon biomedical agents
authors: Genoria AI Team, Yuejie Hou, Yueyuxiao Yang et al.
abstract: Language-model agents now carry out long scientific work in biology, but their judgements about conventions, skills, errors, evidence and stopping are made inside the reasoning that does the work, where they cannot be measured, replaced or improved on their own. Here we present Operon-S1, a fast decision system, a System 1 for the agent, that separates judging from doing. title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
authors: Xuning He, Kai Fan, Runyu Zhang et al.
abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents play an important role in solving complex and sustained tasks, with ever-growing interaction contexts. However, these accumulated contexts will raise substantial computational cost and obscure key decision-relevant evidence. Existing methods typically train external compressors or context-management agents to rewrite context as shorter hard-token sequences, but such external selection may not align with the LLM's evolving representation and is necessarily lossy. authors: Yanchen Liu, Xinyu Che, Brihi Joshi et al.
abstract: Training language-model agents to play long-horizon strategy games is hard because deterministic feedback is sparse and often arrives only at the end of a game. In-game scores can offer dense signals, but they do not reliably predict future outcomes: in 8-68% of position pairs across eight strategy games, the higher-scoring position leads to the worse outcome. title: MEMIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization
authors: Yunhui Jang, Zach Wang, Jai Doshi et al.
abstract: Memory has become central to self-evolving LLM agents, which store and retrieve experience from past rollouts to guide future decisions. Existing systems represent this experience as free-form natural language and maintain it by rewriting, which fits tasks whose experience is narratable. However, in scientific discovery and optimization, experience is often a quantity measured by an oracle under a specific context. title: TraceSpec: Understanding and Improving Speculative Decoding for LLM Agents
authors: Jihao Zhao, Shuaishuai Zu, Pengfei Li et al.
abstract: LLM agents execute tasks through repeated model calls over evolving histories of reasoning, actions, and tool feedback. Aggregate speculative-decoding metrics merge these distinct decisions, providing limited guidance on where draft supervision is needed. We present TraceSpec, a framework connecting trajectory evaluation with adaptive draft training. title: When Disclosure Is Compulsory: Evaluating Ride-Hailing Rebalancing Policies with Self-Interested LLM Driver Agents
authors: Xinyu Wang, Andres Fielbaum
abstract: The EU Platform Work Directive, to be transposed by December 2026, requires ride-hailing platforms to state in plain language the main parameters of their automated decisions and how a worker's behaviour affects them. Such rules are exactly what a large language model (LLM) can read, so drivers will be able to let one decide for them. title: When Should AI Agents Ask? Clarification Requests Under Limited Human Attention
authors: Hanzhao Wang, Shengjie Liu, Zhengchao Wang
abstract: AI agents increasingly carry out delegated tasks in parallel, with one person overseeing several of them at once. In practice, an agent often lacks information its task requires, such as an unstated preference, constraint, or specification. It can ask the human to clarify, or it can search for the information itself, for example in past records, which takes time and effort and may fail. title: How Much Can Tool Calls Reveal About You? Privacy Leakage from Tool-Call Traces
authors: Donghang Duan, Qingyu Liu, Yifei Liu et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents interact with external tools through protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP), producing tool-call traces that may expose behavioral signals about users. In this work, we systematically study the risk of user-profile inference from MCP tool-call traces, where observers infer user attributes from protocol-valid tool interactions without access to user conversations. title: EvoMCP: Co-evolving MCP agents and training data
authors: Xuanang Gao, Kepeng Lin, Xinyan Shi et al.
abstract: Supervised fine-tuning of Model Context Protocol (MCP) agents is typically conducted on a static data distribution, which fails to adapt to the student's evolving capabilities and leaves newly exposed weaknesses insufficiently addressed. title: Cross-Interface Authorization for AI Computer-Use Agents
authors: Genliang Zhu, Chu Wang
abstract: Computer-use agents act through graphical interfaces, command lines, APIs, scripts, and Model Context Protocol servers. A policy decision can be interface-invariant while its executable authorization is not: another route can bypass mediation, alter a security-relevant default, or commit after the authorized state has changed. title: Latent Reasoning in Continuous Space for Unified Multimodal Models
authors: Byungwoo Jeon, Yoonwoo Jeong, Hyunseok Lee et al.
abstract: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) achieve remarkable success on diverse multimodal understanding and generation tasks, yet they still struggle to effectively leverage language-based chain-of-thought reasoning for image generation. As a result, existing reasoning-augmented UMMs often fail to inherit the test-time scaling and fine-grained controllability observed in large language models. title: Subquadratic Attention with a Hierarchical Tree-Structured Indexer
authors: Leon Lufkin, Cutter Dawes, Alexander Speicher et al.
abstract: The quadratic scaling of attention is a fundamental bottleneck limiting the long-context capabilities of large language models (LLMs). A variety of approaches have attempted to circumvent this, but they either fail to match attention's expressiveness (e.g., sliding-window or linear attention variants with fixed-size state) or only achieve constant-factor speedups (e.g., sparse attention methods whose indexers themselves scale quadratically). title: Aligning MLLMs with the Latent Structure of Human Cognition via Behavior-Derived Semantic Dimensions
authors: Ning E, Changde Du, Yizhuo Lu et al.
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance across a wide range of reasoning tasks, yet it remains unclear whether their internal representations and decision criteria align with the latent structure of human cognition. In this work, we propose a novel framework to align MLLMs with the multidimensional mental representations underlying human similarity judgements. title: RECAST: REconstruction of Chain-of-Thought via Auditable Structured Traces
authors: Qi Wang, Kang Xu, Chengcheng Wan et al.
abstract: Large closed-source reasoning models expose only their final answers. The intermediate reasoning that produces those answers is hidden behind API surfaces, tool-call policies, and safety filters. Existing chain-of-thought (CoT) extraction methods assume a side channel: a visible reasoning field, a scratchpad carried through tool calls, or a signed/encrypted reasoning block. title: Stepwise-Querying: Distilling Reasoning without Access to Teacher Chain-of-Thought
authors: Dicong Yu, Wenhua Wang, Tian Wang
abstract: Reasoning distillation is widely used to transfer the reasoning capabilities of large language models to smaller students through teacher-generated supervision. In the black-box setting, however, teachers may expose only final answers and brief solutions, leaving intermediate calculations and validity conditions unavailable and thus limiting the reasoning supervision available for distillation. title: Multimodal In-Context Learning with Explicit Rule Induction
authors: Yuquan Li, Xinyang Jiang, Yuhao Xue et al.
abstract: A central challenge in multimodal in-context learning (MICL) arises from tasks that are ill-defined without context and require uncovering the underlying rules from demonstrations. Existing methods predominantly treat MICL as direct input-output mapping, overlooking the importance of explicitly inducing and reasoning over such rules, limiting both performance and interpretability. title: Breaking Information Islands in Sparse Tuning via Small-World Connectivity
authors: Xianchao Guan, Zijun Xiong, Yifeng Wang et al.
abstract: Sparse tuning is widely used to adapt large language models due to its parameter efficiency. However, its effectiveness depends not only on the number of trainable parameters, but also on the feature-interaction topology of the sparse update's structural support. title: Attention Maps Know When to Think: Training-Free Difficulty-Aware Chain-of-Thought for Reasoning Segmentation
authors: Chanseul Cho, Jaesung Jun, Dongheon Lee et al.
abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has become a standard reasoning strategy in Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs), showing strong performance in complex vision-language tasks such as reasoning segmentation. However, our analysis reveals that indiscriminate CoT usage can lead to degraded performance by inducing unnecessary reasoning, a phenomenon we term overthinking. title: Specification-Guided Generation for Large Language Models
authors: Alessandro Previti, Konstantinos Vandikas, Mario Alviano et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate structured outputs, but existing constrained-decoding methods mainly enforce syntax and cannot directly enforce satisfaction of a formal specification. We introduce a neuro-symbolic, specification-guided decoding framework that combines LLM generation with symbolic reasoning. title: RTL-Interact: Training EDA-Interactive Models for Multi-Task RTL Design
authors: Wenxuan Shi, Yaoyu Zhu, Di Huang et al.
abstract: Large language models offer a promising route to register-transfer-level (RTL) design, but reliable implementations require checking and revision based on electronic design automation (EDA) tools' feedback. Existing RTL-specialized models often lack learned interaction with such EDA tools or rely on separate generation and repair components. title: ImplicitHop: Evaluating knowledge integration across context and memory
authors: Alexander Detkov, Dashiel Karish, Matthew Oleynikov et al.
abstract: The ability to integrate new information and deduce its consequences is central to learning, understanding, and reasoning in large language models (LLMs). Whether information arrives during training or in-context, models must not only store local facts, but propagate their long-range implications globally. To explore information integration in LLMs, we introduce two complementary natural language benchmarks for large-scale evaluation of deductive reasoning as a function of inference depth. The f

title: CIRCE Divines LLM Task Complexity from Constraint Structure
authors: Chenhao Hong, Jiakai Xu, Kaushiki Singh et al.
abstract: Estimating whether a problem is too complex for a large language model (LLM) before the model attempts it can guide model routing, how to allocate test-time compute, and suggest the need for new tools to aid the agent. title: Do Transaction Prices Reflect Visual Preference? A Diagnostic Study with Multimodal Language Models
authors: Fengxian Ji, Jingpu Yang, Fan Zhang et al.
abstract: Existing visual preference evaluation relies on costly human annotations or preference reward models, whereas online marketplace transaction prices are readily available and reflect real purchasing behavior, offering potential low-cost supervision. However, transaction prices conflate visual preferences with non-visual factors such as provenance, demand, and competition, making aggregate accuracy insufficient to distinguish model errors, unreliable price signals, and protocol confounds. title: Latent-Lens: Visual Perception in Small Language Models Through Latent Communication
authors: Mo Shahdloo, Faegheh Sardari, Mathew Salvaris
abstract: Bridging independent vision-language models (VLMs) and small language models (SLMs) in a modular multi-agent system typically forces them to exchange information as discrete text, which creates a lossy bottleneck for spatial and fine-grained details. This constraint is especially acute for SLMs, whose limited capacity makes them more reliant on the quality of the input signal. title: Saidzoda-Tajik-LFM-2.6B: Adapting a 2.6B Hybrid Model to Tajik Tool Calling, and What Continued Pretraining Takes Away
authors: Tohir Saidzoda, Nekruz Maxudov, Bedil Karimov et al.
abstract: We release Saidzoda-Tajik-LFM-2.6B, a Tajik adaptation of the 2.6B-parameter hybrid model LFM2.5-2.6B-Base, built for tool calling in Tajik on modest hardware. The recipe has two stages: LoRA continued pretraining (CPT) on 1,485,319 cleaned Tajik web documents for 3 epochs, then one epoch of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a mix of machine-translated Tajik tool calls, English tool calls kept as replay, and Tajik instructions. title: BYOD: Build Your Own DLM - Efficient Autoregressive-to-Diffusion Language Model Conversion
authors: Ruurd J. A. Kuiper, Robert A. Bagheri
abstract: Unlike autoregressive (AR) models, diffusion language models (DLMs) permit parallel token updates, flexible generation, and bidirectional attention, but leading systems rely on costly pretraining or full-model fine-tuning. We present Build Your Own DLM (BYOD), a generalizable LoRA-only recipe for parameter-efficient AR-to-DLM conversion. title: Enhancing Knowledge Entity Relation Extraction in Abstracts and Full-text Content of Academic Articles Using Large Language Models
authors: Yingyi Zhang, Chengzhi Zhang
abstract: This study investigates the effectiveness of large pre-trained language models (LLMs) for knowledge entity relation extraction (KERE) from academic papers. Existing studies have examined individual types of LLM-based strategies and evaluated model performance using metrics such as precision and recall. title: KV-Cache Patching: Tracing How and Where Fine-Tuned Behaviors Arise
authors: Jonas Loos, Oliver Eberle
abstract: Fine-tuning a language model changes how it responds, but where is this fine-tuned behavior instantiated? To better understand this, we evaluate whether the change in model behavior arises only during the generation of the answer tokens where the change manifests, or whether altered processing of previous tokens causes it via the attention mechanism. title: Counterfactual Pairwise Augmentation Improves Small Pointwise LLM Judges
authors: Mohammad Zangooei, Peyvand Teymoori, Mohammad Robati Shirzad et al.
abstract: Agentic systems increasingly gate individual steps with a pointwise judge that scores a response against a criterion. Small language models are attractive for this role because they can be served and specialized efficiently. Such a judge must locate the criterion's decision boundary, but pointwise labels under-determine that boundary in fine-tuning: labeled responses to different queries differ along many dimensions at once, so they do not reveal which features decide the label. title: HyperRepair: Recovering Forgotten General Capabilities of Fine-Tuned Language Models
authors: Junrong Tang, Jianghui Wang, Hao Kong et al.
abstract: Fine-tuning improves a language model's performance in a target domain but can weaken its general capabilities. Existing methods often face a trade-off between general capabilities and domain specialization, making it difficult to preserve both. We introduce HyperRepair, a framework for recovering general capabilities while retaining domain specialization at only inference cost. title: Predicting Human-Gain Curves under Local Proxy Optimization from Repeated Ratings
authors: Moonwon Choi, Kisung Nam, Seunggeun Lee
abstract: Optimizing a proxy objective can improve human-perceived quality, but the resulting gain can vary with optimization strength. Average proxy-human correlation alone does not reveal how human-perceived quality changes as optimization strength increases. We propose PACE (Proxy Alignment and Curvature Expansion), a pre-optimization diagnostic that uses repeated human ratings to predict the human-gain curve induced by a fixed proxy. title: Precision--Recall Trade-off on the Inference Level for LLMs in Grammatical Error Correction
authors: Ryszard Staruch, Filip Graliński
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently been adopted for Grammatical Error Correction (GEC), achieving strong performance via both full fine-tuning and prompt-based approaches. As probabilistic sequence models, LLMs expose inference-time parameters that directly modify token generation behavior; however, their potential for controlling GEC-specific trade-offs has not been systematically studied. title: A prospective randomized study of patient-centered AI for clinical visit preparation
authors: Xincheng Tan, Matthew Thompson, Xiang Ji et al.
abstract: Patients often arrive at brief, time-constrained clinical visits unsure of what to expect or ask, and millions of adults now turn to general-purpose AI chatbots to prepare beforehand. Yet whether conversational AI improves visit readiness remains unclear. title: Subliminal Reinforcement Learning: traits travel through a judge's scores
authors: Keuntae Kim, Yong Suk Choi
abstract: Subliminal learning, the transfer of a model's trait through data with no semantic trace of it, has been shown for students trained on a teacher's text. Post-training relies on group relative policy optimization with a language-model judge, where the student learns only from its own outputs and one judge's scores. title: MUON-RT Reusing the Teacher's Trajectory for Momentum-Free Muon for LLM Self-Distillation
authors: Aryan Das, Vinay Kumar Verma, Aakansha Mishra
abstract: Self-distillation methods for large language models with an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher already retain a history of student updates. Muon nevertheless stores a separate momentum buffer, increasing persistent training memory. We propose Muon with Reused Teacher (Muon-RT), which reuses the teacher-student displacement to eliminate momentum buffers for hidden weight matrices. title: ACCT: Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer
authors: Yuzhe Liu, Haolin Tian, Tonghan Wang
abstract: In real-world deployments, large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly evolving from single-model invocation toward heterogeneous deployments in which different models are dynamically invoked for inference. When the same context is reused across models, however, each newly selected target model typically has to process it again, repeatedly incurring substantial computational costs. title: Same Question, Different Answers: Auditing Persona-Dependent Variation in Six LLMs on Smoking-Cessation Advice
authors: Artin Yousefi, Aizierjiang Aiersilan, Lorien C Abroms et al.
abstract: Hundreds of millions of people now ask large language model (LLM) chatbots for health advice, which raises a question that is simple to pose and hard to answer: does everyone get the same advice? title: Know When the Equation Is Wrong: Structural Uncertainty for LLM-Guided Symbolic Regression under Extrapolation
authors: Mostafa Cham, Bayu Adhi Tama, Jianwu Wang
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can help discover mathematical equations from data, but most LLM-guided symbolic regression methods focus on a single best equation without quantifying uncertainty over alternative functional forms. This is challenging because distinct equations can fit the observed data similarly while producing substantially different extrapolations. title: ID2Pattern: Pretraining Generalizable Identity Behavior Patterns for Transaction Risk Foundation Models
authors: Ze Zhao, Haoyu Jiang, Weiyu Han et al.
abstract: Large-scale behavioral pretraining offers a promising route to generalizable representations in online payment systems. However, high-cardinality identity fields such as card, device, and account IDs, though rich in behavioral signals, remain underexploited. Their continually growing vocabularies and limited semantic meaning make existing vocabulary-based and semantics-based encodings ill-suited. title: Prune Gradually, Adapt Sparsely: Efficient Pruning of Large Language Models at Extreme Sparsity
authors: Jean Lucien Randrianantenaina, Hung Nguyen, Nasib Ullah et al.
abstract: Weight pruning can reduce the storage and inference cost of large language models (LLMs), but preserving quality at high sparsity levels remains challenging. Existing methods face a quality-cost trade-off in this regime. One-shot pruning is cheap but degrades sharply as sparsity increases, even when followed by post-pruning recovery. title: Chronos-2: A foundation model for multivariate time series forecasting
authors: Abdul Fatir Ansari, Oleksandr Shchur, Jaris Küken et al.
abstract: Accurate forecasting with uncertainty quantification is critical in a variety of scientific applications ranging from epidemiology and economics to energy systems and earth sciences. Yet most forecasting models still need to be developed and trained separately for each domain-specific dataset. Time series foundation models (TSFMs) aim to remove this limitation and enable the application of the same model across domains through large-scale pretraining. title: Structure-Aware Skill Retrieval and Arbitration for Optimization Modeling
authors: Anran Liu, Benzhao Hou, Zongsheng Cao et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can turn natural-language optimization tasks into solver-checked answers, but current agents remain brittle under narrative rewrites and often store reusable experience at the instance level. title: ReX-GG: a LLM Ensemble Pipeline for Relation-extraction and Graph Generation
authors: Giacomo Magnifico, Eduard Barbu
abstract: Current LLM ensemble frameworks focus on multi-step setups with additional modules for answer ranking, often opting for token and span analysis rather than structured outputs, leading to heavyweight architectures with potential fail states along the pipeline. Faster, lighter solutions are more vulnerable to hallucination propagation and can lack output control in more complex pipelines. title: General-purpose foundation models surpass specialized ones on chemical property prediction tasks
authors: Stepan N. Ostarkov, Gregorii A. Semakin, Ivan A. Bespalov et al.
abstract: Foundation models (FMs) learn reusable representations from large collections of unlabeled data. In chemistry the corresponding data mainly consists of molecular structures, which are abundant, whereas experimental measurements are scarce. Chemical FMs such as ChemBERTa and MoLFormer were therefore trained on diverse molecular structures to enable fine-tuning on small experimental datasets (less than 100 datapoints in most realistic scenarios) and subsequent property prediction. title: Automated Keyword Generation Using LLMs in a High-Volume Data Virtualization Service
authors: Saiful Khan, Yiwen Xing, Joyraj Chakraborty et al.
abstract: In modern data infrastructure, a data virtualization service (DVS) allows users to create many versions of source datasets for different processing tasks. For example, a multivariate or multi-modality dataset can be used for different machine learning tasks (e.g., classification, detection, segmentation, forecasting, and so on). title: AI evaluators favor job applications written by certain AI models, independent of candidate quality
authors: Nicolò Pagan, Michael Andreas Ebling, Stefania Ionescu et al.
abstract: Job applicants increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to write cover letters, while employers deploy LLMs to screen them. In this all-AI setting, we ask whether the \emph{choice of model} affects hiring outcomes independently of candidate qualifications. We introduce a multi-model auditing framework pairing eleven LLM writer agents with nine API-hosted evaluator agents across ten job descriptions and fifty candidates per job. Four findings emerge. title: Accurate and Auditable ECG Classification via Visibility Graph Neural Networks
authors: Artur Xavier, Guilherme Henrique Gomes Evangelista, Aitazaz Khan et al.
abstract: Physicians read electrocardiograms (ECGs) from waveform shape and timing, yet accurate deep-learning classifiers rarely show which waveform regions drive their predictions. We introduce LYNX-ECG, a graph neural network that represents each heartbeat as a sparse visibility graph of timestamped turning points. title: Implicit Assumptions About Tasks in Continual Learning
authors: Kathrin Korte, Christian Metzner, Akshay Bedhotiya et al.
abstract: Continual learning is the study of how a model accumulates knowledge from data received over time, rather than all at once. In practice, this is typically achieved by dividing a dataset into tasks and presenting them sequentially. Explanations of the resulting measurements take into account factors such as the similarity between segments, the rate at which the data changes and the order of presentation. title: Task Vectors Can Be Linearly Decomposed into Interpretable and Controllable Components
authors: Yukiya Horiba, Hakaze Cho, Takahiro Yakoh
abstract: Task Vectors (TVs) provide a compact way to steer large language models, but they are typically treated as atomized directions merely extracted from hidden states, leaving their internal functional structure poorly understood. Motivated by prior work that decomposes in-context learning into Task Recognition (TR) and Task Learning (TL), we ask whether a single TV can likewise be decomposed into functionally meaningful components. title: Advancing Clinical Trial Outcome Prediction with Domain-Specific Large Language Models
authors: Burak Bakkar, Hana Moalla, Mohamed Salem Jedidi et al.
abstract: Clinical trial failures are a major barrier to efficient drug development, incurring substantial costs and delaying patient access to effective therapies. Structured approaches such as the Hierarchical Interaction Network (HINT) predict trial outcomes by explicitly modelling interactions between drugs, diseases and protocols, but make limited use of the free text in trial registrations. title: When the Past Shapes Action: Understanding Embodied Memory
authors: Siqi Li, Ziyi Bai, Xinrun Xu et al.
abstract: Recent advances in generative foundation models have expanded the capabilities of embodied AI, enabling increasingly general navigation, manipulation, and long-horizon task execution. However, effective interaction with dynamic environments requires more than only strong perception and reasoning: agents must act with partial knowledge and retain, retrieve, and update information from past observations, actions, and experiences. title: When Steering Shifts Discourse: Identifying and Intervening on Discourse-Level Changes due to Activation Steering in LLMs
authors: Shivam Adarsh, Hetianyu Huang, Lau Safin et al.
abstract: Activation steering is an inference-time technique used to control or modify the behavior, tone, or safety properties of a large language model (LLM) without retraining the model's weights or editing its input prompt, but simply by adding a vector to its residual-stream activations. However, activation steering also changes the generated text in unintended ways, unrelated to intended behavior change, that are not well understood. title: What Should LLMs Forget: Reinforcement Unlearning of Knowledge Associations
authors: Wutong Xu, Yun Qu, Haiyan Feng et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire extensive factual knowledge during pre-training, which may include sensitive, private, or copyrighted information, motivating the development of unlearning methods that selectively remove specific knowledge while preserving general capabilities. title: Multi-Test Nation Bias Benchmarking of LLMs with Explicit Unbiased Baselines
authors: Jonghyeon Choi, Yeonjun Choi, Beakcheol Jang
abstract: While prior work has highlighted that systematic nation-level bias in large language models (LLMs) can pose operational risks for international relations (IR) applications, many existing evaluations still lack a clearly specified unbiased reference (ground truth), limiting fully quantitative and cross-setting measurement. title: From Representation to Readout: Mechanistic Analysis of Membership Signals in Language Models
authors: Wenxi Dai, Jingyu Hu, Yanting Yang et al.
abstract: Membership inference aims to determine whether a particular example was included in a model's training data. Such membership signals are often broadly described as memorization, while the underlying mechanisms can involve both how information is represented internally and how it is accessed by the model to produce behaviors. title: scAnyOmics: Foundation-Model Distillation for Any-to-Any Completion of Multi-omics Virtual Cells
authors: Zhaoqi Song, Ye Du, Yusuke Iwasawa et al.
abstract: Recent advances in single-cell technologies have enabled the profiling of multiple molecular modalities, including transcriptomics, proteomics, and chromatin accessibility, providing a more comprehensive understanding of cellular states. However, integrating heterogeneous modalities and predicting missing molecular information remain challenging, particularly when paired measurements are limited. title: Comparative Evaluation of LLM-Based Review Paradigms for Academic Paper Quality Assessment
authors: Fan Huang, Hongyu Zhou
abstract: Growing submission volumes have renewed interest in using large language models (LLMs) to support peer review. It remains unclear how such evaluation should be structured, how much the model matters, and whether LLM scores predict research impact. We evaluate five paradigms across three input representations and three LLMs on 232 stratified ICLR 2025 submissions. title: From the Zoo to the BULLPEN: Sample-Efficient LLM Profiling via Multi-Channel Model Embeddings
authors: Russell Ro, Qiming Cui, Reza Abbasi-Asl
abstract: Choosing among the hundreds of thousands of available large language models (LLMs) requires a thorough understanding of each candidate model's properties. In practice, each property is measured by its own benchmark suite, so profiling a model on many properties means paying for many separate evaluations. title: LEAP: Efficient LLM Inference Scheduling with Generalizable Length Prediction
authors: Kwan Yan, Jialun Zhong, Yanzeng Li
abstract: Length-aware scheduling reduces request latency in LLM serving by prioritizing shorter requests. However, despite their large model sizes, length predictors can suffer degraded ranking performance under domain and task shifts, and adapting them can require costly retraining. title: With foundation-model features, aggregator complexity does not improve cross-hospital discrimination in gastric whole-slide image classification
authors: Nheng Vanchhay, Ali Hussain, Khan Ziaullah et al.
abstract: Whole-slide image classifiers are usually developed within one hospital and often go untested at unseen hospitals. We assembled 5,036 haematoxylin-and-eosin-stained gastric slides from five Korean hospitals, scanned at 20x and 40x, and compared multiple-instance learning aggregators under leave-one-hospital-out validation on frozen pathology foundation-model features. title: SERIAL-7: Deriving, Realizing, and Preserving Machine-Verifiable Outputs Across Representations
authors: Youngkyung Seo, MiHyeon Kim, Jisoo Lee et al.
abstract: Large language models increasingly generate structured outputs consumed by programs and downstream systems, where semantic correctness alone does not guarantee reliable execution. We introduce SERIAL-7, a Korean-English benchmark built around an executable verification framework for machine-verifiable generation across seven representations.
